1 · Start here

Your respiratory-failure reasoning map

Do not memorize six disconnected diseases. Start with the failed function, then use the gradient and context to localize the problem.

The repeatable exam algorithm

  1. Stabilize first: ABCs. Hypoxemia gets oxygen; fatigue/hypercapnia may need ventilatory support.
  2. Read the ABG: pH → PaCO₂ → PaO₂. Decide whether this is oxygenation failure, ventilatory failure, or both.
  3. Calculate PAO₂ with the alveolar gas equation, then A–a = PAO₂ − PaO₂.
  4. Normal A–a? Think hypoventilation or low inspired O₂ / low barometric pressure.
  5. Widened A–a? Think V/Q mismatch, diffusion limitation, or shunt → now use history, exam, imaging, and pathology.
  6. If ARDS is possible: calculate P/F = PaO₂ / FiO₂, look for bilateral infiltrates, and exclude left-heart failure as the primary explanation.
  7. Match the pattern: DAD ↔ ARDS; fibroblastic airspace plugs ↔ organizing pneumonia; bland alveolar fluid / heart-failure cells ↔ cardiogenic edema.
Professor emphasis: “Get an ABG. Calculate A–a gradient.” The lecture repeatedly uses the gradient to separate pure hypoventilation from intrinsic pulmonary gas-exchange problems.

Fast mental split
Hypoxemic

“Can’t oxygenate”

VDASH: V/Q mismatch, Diffusion limitation, Altitude/low PbO₂, Shunt, Hypoventilation. The A–a gradient separates the last two normal-gradient causes from intrinsic lung problems.

Hypercapnic

“Can’t ventilate”

CO₂ production exceeds clearance. Think severe obstruction, neuromuscular weakness, reduced central drive, or inadequate minute ventilation.

Mixed

“Both”

A COPD patient with pneumonia can be acidemic and hypercapnic and have a widened A–a gradient from parenchymal V/Q mismatch.

5 · Recognition lab

ABG + A–a + P/F calculator

Use the numbers to localize the failure before you chase the diagnosis.

Three lecture-style ABG patterns

Case A

7.48 / 30 / 50

PAO₂ 112 · A–a 62

Acute respiratory alkalosis + widened A–a. Think pulmonary oxygenation failure; lecture case = acute cardiogenic pulmonary edema.

Case B

7.11 / 78 / 50

PAO₂ 52 · A–a 2.5

Acute respiratory acidosis + normal A–a. Think pure hypoventilation; lecture case = narcotic overdose.

Case C

7.28 / 55 / 50

PAO₂ 88 · A–a 38

Acute respiratory acidosis + widened A–a. Mixed ventilatory + gas-exchange failure; lecture case = COPD + pneumonia.

Exam move: A normal A–a gradient tells you the oxygen drop can be explained by what is entering/reaching the alveoli (low pressure or hypoventilation). A widened gradient says oxygen is being lost across the lung because matching, diffusion, or shunt is abnormal.

8 · Exam sheet

One-page-ish final review

1) Respiratory-failure split

Hypoxemic: oxygenation failure. Think VDASH. Treat oxygenation with ↑FiO₂ and, when ventilated, ↑PEEP.

Hypercapnic: ventilatory failure. ↑CO₂ production or ↓clearance. Treat by ↑minute ventilation (RR and/or VT) + cause.

Late fatigue clue: rising CO₂ / slowing respiratory rate in a patient who was working hard.

2) Equations

V̇E = VT × RR

PAO₂ = FiO₂(Patm − 47) − PaCO₂/0.8

A–a = PAO₂ − PaO₂

P/F = PaO₂ ÷ FiO₂

CaO₂ = 1.34(Hb)(SaO₂) + 0.003(PaO₂)

DO₂ = CO × CaO₂

If A–a is…Think
NormalHypoventilation; decreased FiO₂ / low barometric pressure
IncreasedV/Q mismatch; diffusion limitation; shunt
ARDS / DAD
Acute hypoxemia + bilateral opacities + not primarily CHF. P/F ≤300 in Berlin framework. DAD: hyaline membranes → type II proliferation/fibroblasts → possible fibrosis.
Organizing pneumonia
Patchy bronchiolocentric fibroblastic plugs; preserved architecture; migratory infiltrates; often steroid responsive.
Cardiogenic edema
Hydrostatic transudate into alveoli; CHF clues; heart-failure cells in chronic congestion. Can mimic ARDS radiographically.

Professor-style discriminators

  • Somnolent + pinpoint pupils + normal A–a → pure hypoventilation / opioid picture.
  • Barrel chest + wheeze + fever/infiltrate + high CO₂ + widened A–a → COPD + pneumonia mixed failure.
  • 100% O₂ and PaO₂ still very low → shunt-heavy physiology; ARDS is a key context.
  • Migrating opacities after repeated antibiotics → organizing pneumonia.
  • Hyaline membranes → acute DAD. Fibroblastic airspace plugs → OP. Bland pink alveolar fluid → edema.
  • Altitude: FiO₂ stays 21%; Patm falls.
Trap: Do not withhold oxygen from a hypoxemic COPD patient. The lecture explicitly says concern about hypoxemic drive should never prevent supplemental oxygen.

Clarifications / discrepancies

ARDS Berlin criteria — lecture shorthand vs full definition

The lecture slide summarizes ARDS as acute onset, P/F <300, bilateral infiltrates, and not from left-heart failure, with mild/moderate/severe P/F bands. The original Berlin definition is more specific about timing within 1 week, bilateral opacities not fully explained by effusions/collapse/nodules, non-cardiogenic origin, and oxygenation severity assessed with positive pressure (PEEP/CPAP ≥5 cm H₂O, depending on category). The guide keeps the lecture framing for exam alignment and flags the fuller definition here.

JAMA: Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome — The Berlin Definition

ARDS mortality transcript discrepancy

Slide 36 states rapid progression to death at approximately 35%, whereas the transcript text says “around 13%.” Because the slide is internally consistent with the nearby severity-specific mortality figures (27%, 32%, 45%) and the transcript is likely automated speech-to-text, this guide treats 35% as the intended lecture number and does not test the 13% transcription.

Normal PaO₂ range varies within the lecture

One slide lists 85–100 mm Hg; a later evaluation slide lists 80–100 mm Hg, and the instructor also notes age effects. The guide uses the lecture’s anchor value of about 95 mm Hg in a healthy younger person and treats ranges as approximate rather than a single rigid cutoff.
